content: Tendinitis refers to the inflammation, irritation, and swelling of a tendon, which is the fibrous tissue that connects muscle to bone. In many cases, tendon degeneration, also known as tendinosis, may also be present. Symptoms of Tendinitis: Pain and tenderness are typically felt along the tendon, often near a joint. Pain may worsen at night. Pain is exacerbated by movement or physical activity. Causes of Tendinitis: Tendinitis can result from injury, overuse, or the natural aging process, as tendons lose elasticity over time. It may also occur in individuals with systemic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or diabetes. Tendinitis can affect any tendon, but common sites include: The elbow The heel (Achilles tendinitis) The shoulder The wrist High-Risk Groups: Individuals with systemic diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis or diabetes, are at higher risk of developing tendinitis. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider will perform a physical examination, looking for signs of pain and tenderness when the muscle attached to the tendon is used against resistance. Specific tests may be conducted to evaluate specific tendons. The affected tendon may appear inflamed, and the overlying skin could be warm and red. When to Seek Medical Care: Schedule an appointment with a healthcare provider if symptoms of tendinitis develop. Treatment Options: The primary goal of treatment is to alleviate pain and reduce inflammation. Rest or immobilization of the affected tendon is crucial for recovery. This can be achieved using a splint or a removable brace. Applying heat or cold to the affected area can provide relief. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as aspirin or ibuprofen, can help reduce both pain and inflammation. Steroid injections into the tendon sheath may be effective in controlling pain and enabling physical therapy to begin. Physical therapy that focuses on stretching and strengthening the muscle and tendon is essential. This helps restore the tendon’s proper function, promotes healing, and prevents future injuries. In rare cases, surgery may be required to remove inflammatory tissue surrounding the tendon. Where to Find Medical Care: Directions to hospitals or clinics specializing in tendinitis treatment can be sought. Prognosis: Symptoms generally improve with appropriate treatment and rest. If the injury is caused by overuse, modifying work habits may be necessary to prevent recurrence. Possible Complications: Prolonged inflammation increases the risk of further injury, such as tendon rupture. Symptoms of tendinitis may recur. Prevention of Tendinitis: Avoid repetitive motions and overuse of the arms and legs. Maintain strong and flexible muscles. Warm up by exercising at a relaxed pace before engaging in vigorous activities.
